description: We’re a technology-driven team passionate about space exploration, data analysis, and web development. We aim to turn NASA’s open data into interactive tools and meaningful discoveries. Our interests include software engineering, data visualization, AI, and scientific problem-solving. We value collaboration, curiosity, and practical solutions. We work in Arabic and English.
summary: Noor is a free browser game for children aged 7–12 in which they run a small outpost on the Moon or Mars and keep a young astronaut, Noor, safe through real solar storms. Every mission is set on a real space-weather week from NASA's archives. The hour the radiation rose, the scientists' forecast and the readings come from NASA's own recorded data (RadLab LRO CRaTER and Curiosity RAD, DONKI and WSA-ENLIL), so the storm hits at its real hour. Each morning the child plans two jobs: push the mission goal forward or protect Noor. Every choice costs power, air or shielding, and food is a slow background pressure. The forecast can be wrong, just as real ones are, and on Mars Earth's advice arrives late because of the real light-time delay. Noor never dies. Mission Control explains what to try next time, and the Debrief shows "this storm really happened" with the NASA source. The game is Arabic-first with English one tap away, needs no download or account, and comes with a 40-minute lesson plan for teachers. It turns the trade-offs that decide real missions into something a child can feel.
details:
What it does. Noor: Mission Through Real Storms is a turn-based mission simulator. A child picks a mission on the Mission Map. Each mission has one goal (Rock Hunter, Space Gardener, Radiation Detective or Signal Home), a real storm week and a bonus challenge. The mission lasts 5 days on the Moon or 7 sols on Mars. Each morning the child reads a forecast ("Probably not / Maybe / Probably yes") and plans Noor's two jobs: work on the goal, thicken the rocky shield, grow food, fix the air machine, or send the day's report to Earth. Every card costs something. On the Workday clock (08:00–16:00) the storm arrives at the real hour it did in NASA's hourly radiation readings, so the order of the jobs matters: Noor is home before the storm, is caught outside, or finishes a shield layer too late. The evening line names the cause, and the Debrief shows the real readings with their source.

How it uses NASA data. Storm strength and the arrival hour come from the RadLab absorbed dose rate (LRO CRaTER in lunar orbit; Curiosity RAD on the Mars surface). The storm's stages come from DONKI flares, CMEs, particle events and geomagnetic storms, shown in real time order with where each was observed. The morning forecast is a real WSA-ENLIL predicted CME arrival, and the game shows when it was wrong. The Mars message delay comes from JPL Horizons light-time, and site facts and definitions (sol, microgravity, radiation dose) come from NASA science pages. Every value is stored with its unit, URL and access date. Game simplifications are labelled "game scaling" next to the real value, and everything is labelled archived, never live.

Benefits and impact. Children experience real engineering trade-offs instead of just watching them. The game is free, Arabic-first (right to left, Eastern Arabic numerals) with English one tap away, runs on phones and laptops, and needs no download or account; progress stays on the device. Failure teaches without punishment: Noor never dies, and the worst ending is an early trip home with advice for next time. Teachers get a 40-minute lesson plan with a before/after show-of-hands check. Next step: a pilot in Madinah classrooms.

Creativity. The storms aren't invented. A child plays inside a real week, at the real hour, and learns that forecasts can be wrong. Noor and the outpost are living characters: mood, breathing, chest lights, shield thickness and greenhouse plants show the state without numbers. A Scientist view reveals the real units and sources, and a Storm Passport collects a stamp for each real storm survived.

Tools. TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Motion, Recharts, i18next, canvas-confetti, Lucide icons, code-drawn SVG/WebGL art, Vitest (unit, data and simulation tests over thousands of simulated missions) and Playwright (browser tests in Arabic and English, phone and laptop). Python scripts fetch and build the data, and the game is deployed on Cloudflare Workers. Built with Claude Code (Anthropic) as an AI assistant under the team's direction; see docs/AI_USAGE.md.

Factors we considered. Ages 7–12 with plain language; only three gauges (power, air, shield) with food in the background; no "safe" choice without a cost; scientific honesty (no energy bubble, because shielding is mass; CRaTER orbits the Moon; WSA-ENLIL predictions are for Earth); accessibility (big tap targets, reduced motion, a calm storm with no flashing); privacy (no account, no data collected); and offline-friendly archived data.
